bp: This paper starts from a bargain that most web users already know: many sites feel free because advertising pays for them. The usual cost of that bargain is described as privacy, because targeted advertising asks users to give up personal data so ads can be chosen, tracked, and sold more precisely. The paper argues that this is only one bill. A second bill is paid by the user's own device. Ads are not just pictures placed beside content. They bring scripts, tracking calls, consent choices, auctions, and filtering work that make the browser and CPU do extra labor. That labor turns into battery drain, heat, and electricity use. The real-world question is therefore not whether ads are annoying or whether targeting is private. It is how much client-side energy the advertising system moves from advertisers and publishers onto ordinary users who are loading pages, accepting or rejecting banners, and browsing across different devices.
wh: The hard part is that the cost is hidden inside normal browsing. A page with ads, trackers, cookie banners, and real-time bidding still looks like one page visit to the user, even though many separate pieces of code may have run behind it. A simple measurement can easily blame the wrong thing. One website may be heavy because of video, another because of advertising, another because of tracking, and another because of the user's device. Phones, laptops, and other devices spend energy differently, so a result from one machine does not automatically describe the web. User behavior matters too: people scroll, wait, consent, block, or leave. The paper therefore has to model visits realistically, monitor CPU activity, and compare conditions such as consenting to tracking, using ad blockers, and visiting sites that rely on real-time bidding. The central tension is measurement fairness: isolate the advertising cost without pretending the web is cleaner or simpler than it is.
naive: A smart beginner might open a few popular websites, watch the battery meter, and compare pages with and without an ad blocker. That would be tempting because energy sounds physical and direct: load the page, see what power was used, and call the difference the ad cost. The approach fails because battery meters are coarse, pages vary from visit to visit, and background work can blur the result. It also misses the separate roles of consent banners, tracking, real-time bidding, browser-level filtering, and network-level blocking. A few visits on one device would not show whether the effect is stable across many sites and devices. Worse, it might mistake a heavy website for a heavy advertising system. The beginner's method sees a difference, but cannot say what caused it or how general it is.
ap: The paper's core move is to turn web advertising into a measured energy experiment at large scale. Instead of treating the ad ecosystem as an abstract business model, it treats each website visit as a sequence of browser work that can be observed through CPU activity. The authors design a methodology aimed at realistic user behavior, then run 724,994 website visits across diverse devices. They compare energy implications across conditions that matter to users: consenting through cookie banners, blocking ads with browser or network-based tools, and visiting websites that rely on real-time bidding, where ad slots are sold through rapid auctions. The concrete idea is to measure the extra work the user's machine performs when advertising and tracking are present. The paper then summarizes the cost with medians: consent increases energy by 2.57 percent, real-time bidding sites by 33.98 percent, and uBlock Origin reduces client-side energy by 9.62 percent despite its own filtering work.
mech: The mechanism begins with a web visit, not with an advertising theory. A browser loads a site on a particular device. During that visit, the system observes CPU activity, because CPU work is the local signal that the user's machine is spending energy to parse pages, run scripts, process tracking code, handle consent choices, and possibly filter unwanted requests. The input is a large set of visits, 724,994 in the local abstract, spread across diverse devices so the measurement is not tied to one hardware profile. The visit conditions are varied in ways that separate parts of the ad ecosystem. In one comparison, the browser consents through cookie banners, which allows tracking mechanisms to run and reveals the energy cost of that consent path. In another, ads are blocked through browser-based or network-based software, which tests whether the filtering work costs more energy than it saves. In another, websites that rely on real-time bidding are compared with the broader set, exposing the cost of auction and tracking machinery around ad placement. Each visit produces measured CPU behavior. Those measurements are collected, grouped by condition, and summarized with median changes so a few extreme pages do not define the whole answer. The output is not a prediction about one future page. It is an empirical account of how much extra client-side energy is associated with specific advertising choices.
math: The main mathematical idea is careful measurement under comparison. The paper needs to estimate an added cost, so it must ask: compared with what? Energy is not meaningful as a lone number, because every website consumes some energy. The useful quantity is the difference between comparable visits under different advertising conditions. That is a form of controlled empirical estimation: keep the object as similar as possible, change the condition of interest, and measure how the outcome changes. Probability enters because the web is noisy. Any one visit may be unusually light or heavy, but hundreds of thousands of visits reveal a more stable pattern. The median is important because it describes the middle case rather than letting a few extreme pages dominate the story. The mathematical object is therefore a distribution of energy measurements across devices, sites, and conditions. The paper compares those distributions to estimate overhead from consent, real-time bidding, and blocking. There is also a systems budget idea: CPU time is a scarce resource on the user's device, and advertising competes with the user's own browsing for that resource. The tradeoff is free content and targeted ad revenue versus privacy, battery life, and electricity cost. The math fits because the question is not what an ad is supposed to do, but how much measurable work it makes the client perform.
dots: This paper sits in Web analytics because it measures the web as actually experienced by users, but it also connects to the Advertising and E-commerce family in the repo. Many neighboring advertising papers ask how to bid, rank, target, allocate budgets, or detect unsafe ads. This one asks who pays the physical cost of all that machinery. It is a sibling to efficiency and scalability work because the scarce resource is not server time or model memory, but user-side energy. It also touches privacy work: cookie consent is usually discussed as a data permission, yet the paper shows that consenting also changes local energy consumption. Real-time bidding links it to ranking and auction systems, where many parties compete to decide which ad appears. The broader conference pattern is measurement before governance. Before a platform can debate whether an advertising practice is fair, sustainable, or user-respecting, someone has to measure the cost that was previously invisible.
ww: The approach works better than the naive one because it separates a vague complaint into measurable browser work. Ads and trackers are not only network objects that arrive from elsewhere; they trigger local processing. If consenting to tracking permits more scripts or measurement logic to run, CPU activity should rise. If real-time bidding adds auction-related calls and tracking around each ad opportunity, sites that rely on it should impose more work on the client. If an ad blocker prevents enough ad and tracking work, it can save energy even though the blocker itself must inspect and filter requests. The large number of visits matters because web pages are uneven. Some pages will be unusually heavy, and some devices will react differently, but repeated measurement across diverse devices lets the central pattern stand out from page-level accidents. Reporting median changes strengthens that logic by focusing on a typical effect. The paper's causal intuition is physical: code that the client runs consumes CPU work, and CPU work consumes energy. The measurement design makes that hidden path visible.
po: The payoff is a more complete accounting of web advertising. The paper quantifies a cost that is usually left out of the free-content bargain: users pay not only with personal data, but also with energy on their own devices. The local abstract reports three concrete findings. Cookie-banner consent increases energy consumption by a median 2.57 percent across websites and devices. Websites relying on real-time bidding increase median energy consumption by 33.98 percent. uBlock Origin, despite spending energy on filtering, reduces client-side energy consumption by a median 9.62 percent. Those numbers give researchers, browser builders, publishers, and policy discussions a measurable object instead of a vague complaint.
limits: The claims depend on the measurement setup realistically modeling user behavior and on CPU activity being a good enough signal for client-side energy. The abstract says the methodology is designed for realism and uses diverse devices, but it does not prove that every browser, region, network condition, website category, or user habit is covered. The reported medians describe typical changes, not every individual visit. The paper also measures energy cost, not the full value exchange among users, publishers, advertisers, and content access. Blocking results may differ for other blockers or future ad systems. Finally, because the input abstract is about measurement, it supports claims about observed association and comparison, but not a full policy answer about which advertising practices should be allowed.
